questions.question: Explain how a photovoltaic cell produces electricity, why cells are connected in series into panels, and what factors affect a panel's output.
questions.expected_answer: A photovoltaic cell is a thin silicon wafer in two layers treated so that one has spare electrons and the other has spaces, with an electric field across the junction where they meet; photons of light knock electrons loose and the field sweeps electrons to one face and spaces to the other, so a voltage appears and a connected circuit carries current while light falls, with nothing consumed and current stopping harmlessly when light stops. A single cell gives about 0.5 to 0.6 volts regardless of size while its current depends on area and brightness, so panels connect sixty or seventy-two cells in series under toughened glass for thirty to forty volts, and panels are connected in series and parallel for a system's needs. Output is rated in watts under standard full sun, about 400 watts for a common panel, and over a South African day a panel gives four to six times its rating in watt-hours. Efficiency is about twenty percent, with the rest reflected or becoming heat, and heat, dust, wrong angle and shade all reduce output, with shade over a few series cells choking the whole string as a flat cell chokes a torch.

questions.question: Describe the parts of a solar home system and the role of each, narrate a day in the life of the spaza shop system including its weakness, and explain how solar farms and rooftop solar connect to the grid.
questions.expected_answer: The panel makes direct current when lit; the charge controller manages flow into the battery to prevent overcharging by day and deep draining by night; the battery, lead-acid or lithium, stores energy chemically; direct-current loads such as LED lights and phone chargers run from the battery; and an inverter converts twelve or twenty-four volts direct current to 230 volts alternating current for a fridge, television or laptop, with each part sized to the others. At sunrise the panel charges the battery, by mid-morning it also runs the fridge and phone board, a passing cloud drops output to a tenth and the battery covers the gap, by afternoon the battery is full and the controller throttles the panel, at sunset the battery carries lights and fridge through the night and is about half-empty by dawn; a run of rainy days leaves the battery unfilled so the fridge and then the lights are lost, fixed only by a bigger battery or grid back-up. A Northern Cape solar farm's hundreds of thousands of tracking panels feed inverters that push alternating current into the grid at high voltage with no battery because the grid absorbs daytime output, though large batteries are now being added for the evening peak; rooftop solar on houses and businesses works the same way and can feed surplus back where municipalities allow.

questions.question: Set out the advantages and disadvantages of photovoltaic solar cells and state a balanced judgement on solar in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Advantages: free inexhaustible fuel with South Africa receiving over twice Germany's sunshine; no smoke, carbon dioxide, ash or water use in generation; no moving parts and a twenty-five-year life with little maintenance; works anywhere, bringing light and vaccine refrigeration to remote clinics; scales from a lantern to a gigawatt farm; costs down over ninety percent in fifteen years so new solar is cheaper than new coal; and installation jobs spread across the country. Disadvantages: nothing at night, little in cloud and less in winter when heating demand peaks, so storage is needed and batteries are the most expensive and shortest-lived part at five to fifteen years; up-front cost of thousands to tens of thousands of rand beyond the poorest households without subsidy; panels and batteries need mined silicon, silver, lithium and cobalt with environmental and labour costs mostly abroad and recycling barely begun; large farms occupy land; and modest output per square metre keeps cooking and heating expensive. Balanced judgement: solar is the cheapest and cleanest new generation South Africa can build, ideal by day and in remote places and already essential against load shedding, but it must be paired with storage and other sources for night and winter, subsidised for the poorest, and managed for materials and waste.
